Photograph: The Canary View image in fullscreen The Canary website was founded in 2015 against a backdrop of support for the then Labour leader, Jeremy Corbyn. Photograph: The Canary The Canary Canary staff not paid amid fears for news website’s future Outlet faced significant financial challenges after it had funds blocked by bank without explanation Ben Quinn Political correspondent Fri 4 Sep 2026 11.27 EDT Last modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 11.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Workers at the leftwing news outlet the Canary fear it will not survive beyond this year amid access to funds being blocked and allegations of financial mismanagement and internal turmoil. The site, which was founded in 2015 against a backdrop of the wave of support for the then Labour leader, Jeremy Corbyn, appeared set to expand after a multimillion-pound injection of funds last year. But the outlet faced significant financial challenges in July after it announced that it was unable to pay staff and contractors as a result of Lloyds Bank unexpectedly blocking access to “a substantial amount” of its money. The bank did not give a reason. A number of staff at the outlet were not paid again at the end of August. “Any payment difficulties have been solely due to our ongoing debanking issues,” a Canary spokesperson told the Guardian. Some journalists at the Canary, however, believe the banking issues have been used to distract from wider financial mismanagement. They claim the funding, believed to be more than £2m, has been squandered on projects including a short-lived newspaper and the purchase of other websites. Staff at the outlet, where there are about 50 full-time and part-time jobs, have moved to unionise by forming a branch of the National Union of Journalists (NUJ). Over the summer a full staff meeting was told that the new funding had all but gone and they were all facing the possibility of redundancy, with about £400,000 left to see the Canary through to December. Since the Canary faced issues with access to its funds, staff say they have been notified that late payments of pension contributions by the company have been reported by the National Employment Savings Trust (Nest), the government-backed workplace pension scheme that helps employers meet their legal duty of automatic enrolment. It is understood that tensions have also risen after, in the spring, workers say, they were asked by management to sign “non-negotiable” non-disclosure agreements, and told that if they refused they would be subject to changes to their employment contracts. The site describes itself as anti-austerity, anti-Zionist and pro-freedom of expression, among other things. Steve Topple, the outlet’s chief executive, told staff in May that he and others in the management team had serious concerns about the integrity of the Canary as an organisation “and also the level of reputational risk”. “We are at a time when we are doing things that are putting a massive target on our backs, and I am expecting the full force of the system to be placed upon us in due course,” he wrote in a message which also said he would not tolerate the leaking of confidential information beyond the organisation. Staff at the website said in 2022 that they had “overthrown” management, and were now running the organisation as a cooperative. That structure was later dissolved. Some had hoped that the title’s longer term future had been secured after Cecil Hetherington, the founder of the Northern Irish classifieds website Used Cars NI and chair of the house-sale platform PropertyPal, became a major shareholder, contributing an estimated £2m. “We were told originally that Steve had taken on a donation from Cecil Hetherington, but then the ‘debanking’ happened and things changed,” said one worker, referring to the period in which funds were blocked by Lloyds. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion “Payments have been late for the last three months, wages and invoices have been late. Even basic stuff hasn’t been taken care of, with the result that the website went down at one point. “We were told that only about £400,000 was left out of the £2m.” A spokesperson for the NUJ said: “The NUJ’s concern is, and always has been, for the interests of its members and we are working with all our members at the Canary. “We have spoken with Steve Topple and we are working together to ensure the continued stability of the Canary. It’s in that context that we are promoting a constructive relationship.” Topple said: “Lloyds debanked the Canary and closed its account without warning earlier this year, confiscating and holding all of the company’s cash reserves. “This has resulted in severe financial and emotional stress on the company and its employees. We are working through the financial disruption caused by the closure of our bank account and are liaising closely with staff to achieve an equitable balance between meeting our current commitments and safeguarding the organisation’s future sustainability. We have tried to be as open as possible with staff, while balancing the need for confidentiality and avoiding unnecessary upset. “We have undoubtedly made mistakes in our internal communications, and we apologise to everyone in Canary Media Limited and our readers for that. We are currently in discussions with our employees to address their very understandable concerns and would appreciate the privacy to do that.” Explore more on these topics The Canary News websites Newspapers & magazines Trade unions Media unions Digital media London news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Australia World AU politics Environment Climate crisis Indigenous Australia Immigration Media Business Health Science Tech Podcasts Newsletters

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: NSW police arrested an 18-year-old alleged drone operator on Friday over the fatal shooting of Joshua Macdonald earlier in September. Photograph: NSW police View image in fullscreen NSW police arrested an 18-year-old alleged drone operator on Friday over the fatal shooting of Joshua Macdonald earlier in September. Photograph: NSW police New South Wales Alleged drone operator charged with murder after mistaken identity shooting in Sydney NSW police say 18-year-old was operating drone when arrested and likely ‘conducting surveillance on someone or some premises’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Henry Belot Sat 12 Sep 2026 00.37 EDT Last modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 03.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Sydney teenager has been charged with murder after police accused him of operating a drone as part of a suspected botched gang hit in the city’s west. Joshua Macdonald, 40, was shot dead at a Merrylands West home on 2 September in what police believe may have been a case of mistaken identity. He was not known to police and had no links to organised crime. His killing came a day after a seperate mistaken identity shooting in the city, which left 23-year-old university student, Marco Talia, dead in his Glen Alpine home . NSW police on Friday arrested two men, aged 18 and 19. They alleged the younger man was involved in the killing of Macdonald. “A drone was seized and forensically examined by detectives, who allegedly uncovered evidence to suggest involvement in the fatal shooting in Merrylands,” police said in a statement on Saturday. From cleanskins to hitmen: are mistaken identity killings the result of Australia’s ‘crimetasker’ economy? Read more The 18-year-old was charged with murder, participating in a criminal group and contributing to criminal activity and was expected to appear in bail court on Saturday. The 19-year-old was charged with participating in a criminal group, contributing to criminal activity and driving with a suspended licence. He was granted bail in Liverpool local court on Friday and was scheduled to return to court on 24 September. NSW police said the 18-year-old was operating a drone when he was arrested on Friday morning. “That behaviour is obviously of great concern to us,” Det Supt Joe Doueihi told reporters. “It’s more than likely that he was involved in some type of criminality and conducting surveillance on someone or some premises. We are still in the process of identifying who that may have been.” Doueihi alleged the teenager on 2 September was located a few blocks away from the house where Macdonald was killed and used the drone to surveil the area and pass information on to the shooters. He was likely one of a number of people contracted by an organised crime group to carry out parts of the hit, the detective alleged. Other roles contracted out for such a crime can include stealing a car or destroying evidence. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Police at Merrylands West after the 2 September shooting of Joshua Macdonald. Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAP The shooting of Macdonald was at least the fifth suspected NSW mistaken identity killing since May 2025, with fears reckless overseas criminal leaders are ordering the attacks. Senior NSW government ministers have insisted the situation was under control. Last week, the acting NSW premier, Prue Car, said “police are on top of this” . The police minister, Yasmin Catley, echoed that sentiment and said a new criminal model, which allegedly outsourced criminal activities to teenagers, was “very challenging”. “Police are doing everything they can,” Catley said. – with Australian Associated Press Explore more on these topics New South Wales news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://yle.fi/a/74-20246189.text: Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal says he expects Russia to carry out more hybrid attacks across Europe. Michal is among a number of European leaders who have travelled to Rovaniemi at the invitation of Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (NCP) to attend an Arctic summit. Such ambiguous attacks, which fall short of conventional warfare but target the functioning of societies, are intended as a message to Europe, Nato countries and the states bordering the Baltic Sea, according to Michal. Russia wants to discourage European countries from supporting Ukraine, he added, noting that the Kremlin uses a range of proxies and criminal groups to carry out these attacks. Michal told Yle he does not, however, believe Russia is seeking to test Nato's Article 5, which commits members to collective defence. In recent weeks, several Western intelligence services have warned that both hybrid attacks and a limited military strike, for example against the Baltic states, are possible. European leaders in far north Orpo's invitees include German Chancellor Friedrich Merz , Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk , Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen , Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal , Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs , Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda , Romanian President Nicușor Dan and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot . No Swedish leaders are attending because of the parliamentary election held on Sunday. European Council President António Costa and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas are also in Rovaniemi. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Rovaniemi. The Arctic summit is being organised at Finland's initiative. Finland once sought to foster cooperation between the European Union, Russia, Norway and Iceland. Russia has now been excluded from that cooperation and has instead become a threat, which is also being felt in the Arctic. Putting Arctic policy higher on the agenda also means seeking more EU funding for the region. Finland believes the money could, for example, be used to build icebreakers, an area in which it is keen to expand .
